idiom_name: framework / layer-supertype template method driving a lock registry or version check
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: pick the one entry point every business operation must pass through (transactional interceptor, session facade, base-class template method, Unit of Work commit path) and let it acquire the locks the transaction needs - derived from the objects the Unit of Work read and wrote, or from the business-transaction id. Release happens in the same place on commit, rollback, timeout and abort. Keep the mechanism itself (lock table, version column, mutex registry) behind an interface so the policy can change without touching business code, and provide a declarative opt-out (read-only, no-lock, narrower or wider scope) because a rule with no exceptions gets bypassed. The classic hand-written form - each business method calling acquire and release itself - is justified only when there is a single such method or the framework cannot be changed.
code_sketch:
class BusinessService(LayerSupertype):                  # the one entry point
    def execute(self, operation, business_tx_id):
        with self.locks.acquire_for(business_tx_id):     # framework decides the lock set
            result = operation(self.unit_of_work)        # no lock calls in business code
            return self.unit_of_work.commit(result)      # release on commit/rollback/timeout
pitfalls: A framework hook that nobody is forced to use is not an implicit lock: if a caller can reach the data without passing the entry point, the scheme has a gap.
Defaulting to one exclusive lock for every operation converts rare conflicts into permanent contention.
Framework-acquired locks still need an owner, a timeout and a release path on abort; implicit acquisition must not hide an unbounded wait.

Relying on implicit session-level locks (Hibernate's implicit READ/WRITE LockMode) without explicit configuration means the lock mode depends on the persistence context state, making it invisible and non-portable.

PESSIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT in Hibernate bumps the version on lock acquisition even when the entity is not modified, causing spurious version conflicts on subsequent transactions — use it deliberately.

In Spring, private @Transactional methods are silently ignored; in .NET, TransactionScope methods on interfaces must be virtual or called through the interface — framework hooks that look implicit but fail silently.
An ORM flush mode of AUTO can trigger a flush (and lock acquisition) inside a read-only transaction when a flush is not expected, invalidating the assumption that read-only transactions never block.
Framework-level lock timeouts (lock_wait_timeout) propagate as database exceptions; if the exception is swallowed or retried without backoff, the lock timeout becomes a denial-of-service vector.
Optimistic locking without a retry strategy turns a conflict into a silent data loss event when the client catches and suppresses the exception rather than surfacing it.

Wrong move: Call a Spring @Transactional method through self-invocation -> proxy interception is bypassed, so the intended transaction or lock boundary may never run -> instead route the call through a proxied bean or enable AspectJ weaving.

Wrong move: Treat an EF Core concurrency token as a pessimistic lock -> SaveChanges detects a stale write but does not reserve the row while business work proceeds -> instead choose an explicit provider-supported pessimistic lock when waiting must be prevented.

Wrong move: Request a Hibernate pessimistic LockMode outside a transaction -> the database lock cannot have the intended transaction lifetime and may be rejected or released too early -> instead acquire the lock inside the short framework-owned transaction.
